svg.title: Scenario: a flash sale sends 30x normal traffic
svg.text: Scenario: a 10:00 flash sale. Traffic goes from 2,000 to 60,000 requests a second in under a minute.
Every layer exists to make sure the next one sees less traffic than the one before. Spanner and the PSP should never see the spike, only a steady stream.
Requests per second reaching each layer at the peak (illustrative numbers)
Before 10:00 (the part that decides how it goes)
Load test at 1.5x the forecast a week before, same code, same data size
Raise quotas early: GKE nodes, Spanner compute, Cloud Run instances
Pre-scale: HPA minReplicas up at 09:30, Spanner capacity up at 09:00
Warm the CDN: request every sale page once, long max-age + versioned URLs
Freeze deploys from 09:00 to 12:00, feature flags only
Turn on Cloud Armor rate limits and bot rules in preview first, then enforce
Waiting room hands out tokens at the rate checkout can take, not faster
Hold stock in Spanner when the item goes in the basket, with a TTL
Respond "order received" after the Spanner commit; the rest is async
Shed non-essential features first: reviews, recommendations, wishlists
Watch checkout success rate and p95, not CPU
If the PSP slows down, queue the authorise call, do not retry in a loop
The hot SKU problem: 5,000 shoppers buying the same TV in the same second
Every checkout locks the same row. Transactions queue, abort and retry.
Latency climbs, throughput tops out at what one row can take.
Pick a random shard (or the shopper id hash), decrement it, try another if it is empty.
Total stock = sum of shards. Contention drops by the number of shards.
Other ways to get the same effect
- Reservation tokens: pre-mint 500 tokens into a Valkey list, LPOP one per shopper, then write the order to Spanner. No token, no checkout.
- Batch allocation: checkout writes a reservation request; one worker per SKU drains them in order and allocates in batches of 50.
- Whatever you pick, Spanner stays the source of truth. A lost Valkey token just means one unit sells a few minutes late, never twice.
- Use a UUIDv4 or bit-reversed sequence for order ids, never a timestamp or a plain counter, or the order table gets a hotspot too.
